## 1. The subdomain list

> Here are the 8 subdomains under `earth-climate`. What is missing? What is a distinction nobody in your field actually makes? What are we calling by the wrong name?

(03 §12.2, ask 1.) The family: Benchmarks whose subject is the Earth system or a process within it.

- Included: Tag this as PRIMARY if the scored quantity is weather, climate, land surface, hazard, ecology or energy in a geophysical setting.
- Excluded: Do NOT tag this if the subject is a generic vision task that happens to use satellite imagery, and do NOT tag it where the physical process is studied outside an Earth-system context, which is \`physics\`. A vision task is generic when the benchmark's claim is the vision method and its labels are objects that merely appear in overhead imagery (buildings, vehicles, animals). Where the labels are Earth-system quantities (land cover, surface water, crops, biomass, ice), or the benchmark presents itself as Earth observation, this family is primary and the vision task subdomain is secondary, however standard the vision task.

### 2.1 S2S AI Challenge (s2s-ai-challenge)

`data/benchmarks/earth-climate/s2s-ai-challenge.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*Tercile probabilities of 2 m temperature and precipitation for weeks 3-4 and 5-6 of 2020, scored by RPSS over land.*

A prize competition run in 2021 by the WWRP/WCRP Subseasonal to Seasonal Prediction Project (S2S Project) of the World Meteorological Organization, with the Swiss Data Science Center (SDSC), which hosted the code on its RenkuLab platform, and ECMWF, which served the data from the European Weather Cloud. Entrants issue probabilistic forecasts of biweekly 2 m temperature and total precipitation for weeks 3-4 and 5-6, as probabilities of the below-, near- and above-normal terciles on a global 1.5-degree grid, for the 53 Thursdays of 2020. They may train on reforecasts of 2000-2019 and real-time 2020 forecasts from ECMWF, ECCC and NCEP and on any public data dated before each forecast, most often to post-process the dynamical models' output. A scoring bot computed the ranked probability skill score (RPSS) against a climatological forecast from NOAA CPC observations, averaged over land between 90N and 60S, both variables and both lead times; prizes (CHF 30,000 in all) required beating climatology and a re-calibrated ECMWF benchmark (RPSS -0.0016). Of 47 registered teams, 10 submitted and 5 beat both; the winners, from CRIM with ECCC, BSC and the University of Connecticut, reached 0.046, 0.029 and 0.006. The 2020 observations were public throughout, so the rules required open code, overfitting safeguards and peer review. The competition is over, its scorer has stopped and its repositories moved from RenkuLab to GitHub in December 2025. ChaosBench, the other subseasonal entry, scores daily reanalysis fields of 124 variables to 44 days ahead for data-driven emulators instead.

#### s2s-ai-challenge · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary earth-climate/weather-forecasting · [S1][s2s-ai-challenge-s1]
  - why: Forecasts are issued on stated start dates (each Thursday of 2020) for stated lead times, weeks 3-4 and 5-6, in the subseasonal range, and scored against observations; there are no emissions or forcing scenarios. That is the leaf's inclusion test, which runs up to the subseasonal-to-seasonal range, as for chaosbench, its example.
  > The objective of the competition is to improve week 3-4 (weeks 3 plus 4) and 5-6 (weeks 5 plus 6) subseasonal global probabilistic 2m temperature and total precipitation tercile forecasts issued in the year 2020 by using Machine Learning/Artificial Intelligence.
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S2][s2s-ai-challenge-s2]
  - why: Systems predict the state of the atmosphere at the surface, fortnightly mean temperature and accumulated precipitation, and are scored against observations.
  > using observed gridded data from NOAA Climate Prediction Center (CPC)
- `capability` = calibration-uncertainty · [S1][s2s-ai-challenge-s1]
  - why: The submission is a probability for each tercile, and the ranked probability score consumes those probabilities; the climatological forecast it is compared with assigns a third to each.
  > This RPS is compared to the climatology forecast in the Ranked Probability Skill Score (RPSS).
- `evaluation_method` = uncertainty-calibration-score · [S1][s2s-ai-challenge-s1]
  - why: The ranked probability score is a proper scoring rule applied to the emitted tercile probabilities, and RPSS its skill score against climatology, which the term covers even where a discipline has standardised the rule under its own name. The gridded RPSS is clipped to \[-10, 1\], latitude-weighted over land and averaged over both variables and both lead times.
  > This RPS is compared to the climatology forecast in the Ranked Probability Skill Score (RPSS).
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model, classical-algorithm · [S2][s2s-ai-challenge-s2]
  - why: Entrants are models trained on the challenge's reforecasts for a task meteorology defines, the calibration and combination of subseasonal forecasts (CNNs, random forests, logistic regression, EMOS), which domain-specialist-model admits as trained from scratch for a task the discipline defines. The re-calibrated ECMWF forecast, a physics-based model with tercile edges from its own reforecast climatology, is scored against the observations like an entrant and serves as the benchmark to beat, which classical-algorithm admits as a baseline. The site asks for machine learning, and the scored list also holds a Bayesian statistical-dynamical post-processing entry.
  > The competition encouraged the use of AI methods on forecasts and reforecasts from models in the S2S database to provide better calibration and multimodel ensemble combination
- `evaluation_target` = learned-system · [S1][s2s-ai-challenge-s1]
  - why: The competition asks for machine learning or artificial intelligence; the re-calibrated ECMWF forecast and climatology are the references entrants must beat, not the systems under test.
  > The ML-based forecasts should beat the re-calibrated real-time 2020 ECMWF and climatology forecasts to be able to win prizes

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `probabilistic-forecasting` · [S1][s2s-ai-challenge-s1]
  - why: The outcomes already existed. The organisers chose 2020, a past year, over a real-time competition, and its observations were public during the competition, so the truth was not even withheld; the term's exclusion test removes an answer that already exists. The probabilistic half is calibration-uncertainty.
  > The organizers explicitly choose to run this competition on past 2020 data, instead of a real-time competition
- `evaluation_method` not `expert-panel-assessment` · [S1][s2s-ai-challenge-s1]
  - why: The rules made the final ranking the average of the RPSS rank and an expert review rank, but the review was made pass/fail before it ran, passed all five, and the prizes followed the RPSS leaderboard.
  > The expert peer review gave a pass on all five submissions. Based on the leaderboard the prizes go to:
- `designed_for_subjects` not `scientific-surrogate-model` · [S1][s2s-ai-challenge-s1]
  - why: Methods that replace dynamical models were allowed (the site's approach I predicts from initial conditions), but the competition was built for post-processing, the winners all post-processed ECMWF output or used observations, and entrants are scored against observations rather than against a simulator they emulate.
  > Predict the week 3-4 & 5-6 state based on: I. the initial conditions (observations at forecast\_time) II. the week 3-4 & 5-6 S2S forecasts

WMO and ECMWF are intergovernmental bodies, but no source read calls them public bodies, and the code repositories sit in the contractor's personal account, which the individual term's holder test would read as key-person risk; ECMWF holds the data.

The entrants post-process dynamical forecasts; a forecast-verification specialist may read a calibrated forecast system as standing in for the forecast system, which would bring the \`forecasting\` profile and its lead\_time and resolution\_window into force.
6. (field `ground_truth_source`) ground\_truth\_source held-out-labels follows cy-bench for observed labels, although the 2020 observations were public and not held out; experimental was the alternative for CPC's gauge and station analyses.
7. (field `data.dataset_licence`) dataset\_licence is null. The challenge data are a subset of the S2S database at ECMWF, whose terms were not read, and the CPC observations come through IRIDL; neither licence was found in the sources read.
8. (field `data.access`) data.access fully-open rests on the climetlab README and an object-store index that answered a HEAD request; no file was downloaded, and the RenkuLab datasets' git LFS objects may not have moved to GitHub, which the old gitlab.renkulab.io host (timed out on 2026-11-04) cannot confirm.

By chaosbench's pattern they would hold lead\_time "weeks 3-4 (14 days) or weeks 5-6 (28 days), or both averaged" and training\_data\_policy "any public data before each 2020 start date".

### 2.2 ClimSim (climsim)

`data/benchmarks/earth-climate/climsim.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*Emulate a multi-scale climate model's subgrid physics column by column, offline and coupled back into the host model.*

A dataset and benchmark for machine-learning parameterizations of subgrid atmospheric physics (storms, clouds, turbulence, rainfall and radiation) for hybrid ML-physics climate models. The data are E3SM-MMF simulations, in which a cloud-resolving model nested in every grid column of a host climate model resolves convection: the inputs are one column's macro-scale state and boundary conditions before the nested calculation, and the targets are the tendencies it produces and the surface fluxes the land model needs, saved every 20 minutes for ten simulated years of present-day climate. Three simulations are released: high resolution with real geography (21,600 columns, 5.7 billion samples, 41.2 TB), and low resolution (384 columns, 100 million samples each) with real geography or as an aquaplanet. Offline, emulators are scored per variable by MAE and R2 (with CRPS in the SI) on the last two simulated years; the paper's six baselines are an MLP, a CNN, an encoder-decoder, heteroskedastic regression, a randomized prior network and a conditional VAE. ClimSim-Online (v6, 2024) adds a containerized workflow that couples a TorchScript emulator into E3SM-MMF and scores the hybrid run's monthly RMSE and zonal-mean bias against a reference simulation; the MLP baseline crashed within two months, while the maintainers' U-Net with cloud physics constraints ran stably for at least five years. A Kaggle competition in 2024 (693 teams, $50,000 in prizes) scored one weighted R2 on hidden rows of the low-resolution data with the full variable list, and a 2026 follow-up couples the winning teams' architectures online.

#### climsim · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary earth-climate/climate-projection; secondary physics/simulation-surrogates · [S1][climsim-s1]
  - why: The scored quantities are the atmosphere's subgrid tendencies in a climate model, so the family is earth-climate. No leaf names the emulation of a climate model's physics (a tag-gap is logged). climate-projection is the nearest, since the stated goal is better climate models for long-term projections, but its definition asks for projections under stated emissions or forcing scenarios, and ClimSim has one present-day climate (2005-2014 climatological boundary conditions) and no scenario (see review\_checks).
  > with the ultimate goal to help improve the performance and accuracy of climate models used for long-term projections.
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S1][climsim-s1]
  - why: An emulator predicts the tendencies the nested cloud-resolving model produces for an atmospheric column, and is scored against the simulator's output, offline per sample and online through the climate statistics of the coupled run.
  > The target vector contains the tendencies of the same state variables representing the impact of unresolved processes
- `evaluation_method` = statistical-fit · [S1][climsim-s1]
  - why: Offline, MAE and R2 per output variable, computed at each location and level and averaged; online, monthly mass-weighted RMSE and multi-year zonal-mean bias of the hybrid run against the reference E3SM-MMF run; on Kaggle, R2 on weighted predictions. All are goodness-of-fit statistics on continuous fields.
  > The mean absolute error (MAE) and the coefficient of determination (R2) are calculated independently at each horizontal and vertical location
- `designed_for_subjects` = scientific-surrogate-model · [S1][climsim-s1]
  - why: The entrants are learned parameterizations that stand in for the nested cloud-resolving simulator and are scored against what it produced, offline and when coupled to the host model.
  > ClimSim is unique for its focus on learning ML parameterizations which can be used in hybrid climate simulations.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `earth-climate/weather-forecasting` · [S1][climsim-s1]
  - why: Nothing is forecast from initial conditions at a lead time and scored against observations. Offline, each sample is one 20-minute model step of one column; online, a hybrid run is scored on monthly and multi-year climate statistics against a reference simulation.
  > These data were saved at 20-minute intervals (i.e., the time step of the host climate model) for 10 simulated years
- `capability` not `calibration-uncertainty` · [S1][climsim-s1]
  - why: Three baselines are stochastic (HSR, RPN, cVAE) and the SI reports CRPS for all models, but the paper's tables and figures, the online metrics and the Kaggle score all score point predictions; CRPS is supplementary (see review\_checks).
  > We also report continuous ranked probability scores (CRPS) for all considered models in SI.
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S1][climsim-s1]
  - why: The test split is the last two years of the same present-day simulation, after a one-month gap; the paper says climate change is absent from this version, and no shifted condition is scored. Online runs can drift out of sample, but that is scored as error, not as a condition of its own.
  > Although the impacts of global climate change and inter-annual variability are absent in this initial version of ClimSim
- `evaluation_method` not `uncertainty-calibration-score` · [S1][climsim-s1]
  - why: CRPS consumes the stochastic baselines' distributions, but it is reported in the SI only; the headline offline, online and Kaggle scores are on point predictions. Tagging it would also resolve the forecasting profile, whose lead time does not exist here.
  > We also report continuous ranked probability scores (CRPS) for all considered models in SI.
- `evaluation_method` not `simulation-rollout` · [S1][climsim-s1]
  - why: The online evaluation runs the emulator inside a climate simulator, but no policy acts and no episode is scored on a bounded scale; the hybrid run's climate statistics are compared with a reference run's by RMSE and bias.
  > Climate statistics in these hybrid simulations are evaluated against those from pure physical E3SM-MMF simulations.

**Open review checks** (11):

1. (field `domain`) climate-projection or another home. ClimSim has no emissions or forcing scenarios (one present-day climate, 2005-2014 boundary conditions), which the leaf's definition asks for; it is filed there as the nearest leaf for climate-model emulation, and a tag-gap proposes a leaf for it. physics/simulation-surrogates as primary was considered; the family exclusion test keeps an Earth-system process in earth-climate. · [S1][climsim-s1]
   > which have been generated to reflect a climatological average of the 2005-2014 period
2. (field `versions`) One entry for three protocols (offline v1, the Kaggle edition, ClimSim-Online). Whether the Kaggle competition, with its own variable list, hidden rows and single weighted R2, should be its own entry, and whether version\_kind edition fits a one-off competition.
3. (field `aggregation_policy`) aggregation\_policy official-aggregate rests on the Kaggle score. The paper reports each variable apart and the online metrics have no aggregate, so none-by-design or unknown are defensible for the paper's protocol.
4. (field `evaluation_method`, needs a specialist) calibration-uncertainty and uncertainty-calibration-score are rejected because CRPS is SI-only; the stochastic baselines (HSR, RPN, cVAE) emit distributions, and a reviewer may read CRPS as part of the protocol.
5. (field `governance.independence_flags`) \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\] · [S1][climsim-s1]
   > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
6. (field `activity`) activity closed assumes Kaggle's late-submission route, if open, does not count. The competition pages and record read do not say whether late submissions are accepted.
7. (field `execution.reproducibility_tier`) reproducibility\_tier automatable-with-simulator and compute\_tier simulator-required follow the online evaluation; if the offline R2 is taken as the headline, fully-automatable and a GPU tier would apply.
8. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) ceiling\_anchor\_type theoretical-maximum is for the offline and Kaggle R2; the online errors are read against internal unpredictability from reruns of the reference simulation, a noise-ceiling for those metrics. · [S1][climsim-s1]
   > Additionally, to estimate the inherent unpredictability of the atmospheric system, we ran three additional pure physical simulations with the same initial conditions.
9. (field `events`) The paper says several thousand participants entered the Kaggle competition; Kaggle's record gives 877 competitors in 693 teams (5,177 users joined), and the follow-up says about 700 teams. The entry uses Kaggle's counts. · [S1][climsim-s1]
   > global participants in a Kaggle ML competition based on the ClimSim dataset
10. (field `lifecycle`) Current use beyond the maintainers is thin. The follow-up is by the maintainers' group, and the November 2025 abstract's last author is a ClimSim author; an independent 2025-2026 result was not found through arXiv's and OpenAlex's searches (Semantic Scholar's API refused with 429). The follow-up also says ClimSim holds a single climate and that a new dataset may be needed, which may signal a successor. · [S4][climsim-s4]
   > Unfortunately, ClimSim only contains data from a single climate.
11. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type academic-lab follows chaosbench for LEAP's organisations; LEAP is an NSF centre spanning several institutions and the README calls the authors a consortium, so community-collective is the alternative. · [S9][climsim-s9]
   > developed by a consortium of climate scientists and ML researchers

### 2.3 CropHarvest (cropharvest)

`data/benchmarks/earth-climate/cropharvest.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*Crop-type and cropland classification of single-pixel satellite time series in four regional tasks, by AUC ROC and F1.*

A global dataset of geo-referenced agricultural labels paired with satellite pixel time series, with benchmark tasks, released by NASA Harvest and the University of Maryland with a NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks paper and the cropharvest Python package. The paper's release harmonises 90,480 labels from 20 datasets, each with a crop or non-crop label and about a third with a finer agricultural class; the current release holds 95,186 from 21 datasets. Each label is a point or a polygon's centroid, and its input is the nearest pixel's one-year series of 12 monthly steps and 18 bands: Sentinel-2 bands and NDVI, Sentinel-1 VV and VH, ERA5 precipitation and temperature, and SRTM elevation and slope, all resampled to 10 m. The paper defines three binary tasks in different agroecologies with small training sets: maize against the rest in Kenya, coffee against the rest in Brazil, both scored on every pixel of test polygons in held-out bounding boxes, and crop against non-crop in Togo, scored on 306 points. The package later added a fourth, crop against non-crop in China. Scores are AUC ROC and F1 at a 0.5 threshold, averaged over ten seeds; the paper's baselines are a random forest and an LSTM initialised randomly, by crop/non-crop pre-training on the rest of the dataset, or by MAML. There is no leaderboard; Earth-observation foundation model papers report the tasks in their own work, some by accuracy.

#### cropharvest · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary earth-climate/remote-sensing; secondary earth-climate/agriculture · [S3][cropharvest-s3]
  - why: A model reads crop type, or cropland, off a satellite pixel time series. Crops are among the Earth-system labels the remote-sensing inclusion test names, and the benchmark presents itself as a remote sensing dataset, so remote sensing is primary.
  > CropHarvest is an open source remote sensing dataset for agriculture with benchmarks.
- `capability` = perception · [S4][cropharvest-s4]
  - why: The input is a raw satellite signal, a pixel's multispectral, radar, weather and elevation series, and the score measures the crop class recovered from it.
  > For each label, a one-year time series with 12 timesteps is constructed, each representing an aggregated value over 30 days.
- `evaluation_method` = classification-metric · [S4][cropharvest-s4]
  - why: AUC ROC and F1 at a 0.5 threshold, general statistics of the score ranking and the confusion matrix, which classification-metric's inclusion test names.
  > We report the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC ROC) and the F1 score using a threshold of 0.5 to classify a prediction as the positive or negative class.
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model · [S4][cropharvest-s4]
  - why: The benchmark compares models trained for crop-type mapping, a task Earth observation defines, from random forests to LSTMs pre-trained on the global dataset; its current entrants are Earth-observation foundation models probed on the tasks.
  > We evaluated the performance of three neural network models and a random forest model on the benchmark tasks.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `vision/classification` · [S3][cropharvest-s3]
  - why: As secondary. The leaf assigns a whole image to categories, and CropHarvest's item is one pixel's 12-step series of 18 bands, with no spatial extent. No vision task subdomain fits single-pixel time series, so none is recorded.
  > The shape of \`x\` represents 12 timesteps and 18 bands.
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S4][cropharvest-s4]
  - why: The paper names domain shift in space as a challenge the dataset enables, but each task trains and tests in the same region. The Kenya and Brazil test polygons sit in bounding boxes inside the region the training data cover and are removed from training to avoid spatial autocorrelation, and Togo's test points come from the same dataset as its training set. No task scores inputs drawn deliberately from a distribution the model was not fitted to.
  > We removed the test polygons from the training sets to ensure there was no spatial overlap between the training and test sets
- `capability` not `transfer-learning` · [S4][cropharvest-s4]
  - why: The paper's stronger baselines pre-train on the rest of the global dataset (crop/non-crop or MAML) and fine-tune on each task, but that is an entrant's training choice; the benchmark scores each regional task the same way whatever the entrant trained on, and reports no transfer as a condition of its own.
  > We used the entire dataset for training, excluding the test tasks.
- `capability` not `sample-efficiency` · [S4][cropharvest-s4]
  - why: The tasks were chosen across training-set sizes, and the Togo task adds a curve over subsampled training sets, which the paper calls an additional experiment. But entrants may train on the other ninety thousand labels as well, so no budget of labelled samples is fixed, and the headline scores are at the full task training sets.
  > We evaluated the models after training on a range of sizes subsampled from the original training dataset
- `evaluation_method` not `exact-match` · [S5][cropharvest-s5]
  - why: Plain accuracy, a mean of per-item verdicts, is how one 2026 user reports the Togo and China tasks (as\_used), not the benchmark's metric.
  > and accuracy (CropHarvest)
- `designed_for_subjects` not `classical-algorithm` · [S4][cropharvest-s4]
  - why: The random forest is the paper's conventional remote sensing baseline, but a tree ensemble is a trained model, which the term's exclusion names.
  > Random forests are commonly used for remote sensing tasks

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `domain`, needs a specialist) Primary domain remote-sensing, with agriculture secondary. Crops are a remote-sensing label by that leaf's inclusion test, and agriculture's examples are predicted outcomes; a specialist may read crop-type mapping as an agricultural outcome and swap the two. · [S3][cropharvest-s3]
   > CropHarvest is an open source remote sensing dataset for agriculture with benchmarks.
2. (field `domain`) No vision task subdomain is recorded, because the items are single-pixel time series, not images. Whether a time-series classification method subdomain is missing from the taxonomy, or vision/classification should stretch to cover it, is a taxonomy question.
3. (field `capability`) distribution-shift-generalization was rejected because each task trains and tests in the same region. The paper frames spatial domain shift as a challenge, and the regional tasks could be read as held-out sites for a model pre-trained on the rest of the globe. · [S4][cropharvest-s4]
   > handling domain shift in space (regional differences in agriculture and climate)
4. (field `capability`) sample-efficiency was rejected; the tasks were chosen across small training-set sizes (21 coffee positives in Brazil) and Togo carries a training-size curve. Tag it if the task training sets count as fixed budgets although entrants may pre-train on the rest. · [S4][cropharvest-s4]
   > enable comparison of machine learning models in a wide range of agroecologies and in-distribution dataset size regimes
5. (field `subsets`) The China task rests on config.py and the README's description of a task with no target label; no source read gives its size, its labels' origin or its first release. TESSERA v2 scores it as a crop/non-crop task. Whether it counts as part of the benchmark or as a package extension. · [S8][cropharvest-s8]
   > TEST\_DATASETS = {"Togo": "togo-eval", "People's Republic of China": "china-crop"}
6. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type academic-lab rests on background knowledge that NASA Harvest is led from the University of Maryland; no source read states who holds the nasaharvest organisation or NASA Harvest's form.
7. (field `paper`) The paper has no DOI and its only read copy, the proceedings PDF, is withheld from archiving for the authors' e-mail addresses, so every paper quote rests on a Source with no capture. The OpenReview copy (forum JtjzUXPEaCu) refused the request.
8. (field `aggregation_policy`) aggregation\_policy none-by-design rests on the paper reporting each task separately and choosing them to be distinct; the paper does not say in words that no aggregate is intended. unknown is the alternative.
9. (field `versions`) v14 is recorded as non-breaking by default. The paper promises unchanged task definitions, but the training pool grew from 90,480 to 95,186 labels, which changes what a pre-trained entrant sees; v9 to v13 were not read. · [S4][cropharvest-s4]
   > As new datasets are added, new benchmark tasks may also be added but existing task
10. (field `data.dataset_licence`) The dataset licence changed from CC BY 4.0 (Zenodo v1) to CC BY-SA 4.0 (v8 and the paper); the repository applies CC BY-SA 4.0 to the code as well. · [S2][cropharvest-s2]
   > "rights":"Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International"

### 2.4 GEO-Bench (geo-bench)

`data/benchmarks/earth-climate/geo-bench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Pretrained Earth-observation models fine-tuned on satellite and aerial tasks: 12 in GEO-Bench, 19 in GEO-Bench-2.*

A benchmark for pretrained models on Earth observation, built from public remote-sensing datasets that the maintainers modified, subsampled and re-split. The 2023 edition, GEO-Bench, has six image classification and six semantic segmentation tasks (detection and counting datasets were turned into segmentation), from multispectral, SAR, hyperspectral and elevation data at 0.1 to 30 m per pixel. Users fine-tune a backbone on each task within 16 hyperparameter trials, repeat the chosen setting over at least ten seeds, and report normalised scores aggregated by interquartile mean with bootstrapped confidence intervals. GEO-Bench-2 (2025; TMLR 2026, per its README's citation) is the successor: 19 datasets across classification, pixel-wise regression, semantic segmentation, object detection and instance segmentation, three of them carried over from GEO-Bench, ranked in nine overlapping capability groups (among them datasets under and at or above 10 m ground sample distance, RGB/NIR against multispectral, and multi-temporal), with a Hugging Face leaderboard fed by pull requests. Each task keeps its source dataset's sensor and resolution, which the paper's own ablation shows moves the scores; the GEO-Bench README now recommends GEO-Bench-2 instead.

#### geo-bench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary earth-climate/remote-sensing; secondary vision/classification, vision/segmentation, vision/detection; per_edition true · [S3][geo-bench-s3]
  - why: Models extract information from satellite and airborne imagery, and the benchmark presents itself as Earth observation, which the remote-sensing term makes primary although some labels are objects seen from above (cattle, birds, buildings); the term sends the vision tasks to secondary.
  > Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) are transforming Earth Observation (EO), but evaluation lacks standardized protocols.
- `capability` = perception · [S4][geo-bench-s4]
  - why: Every task scores what a model recovers from an image or image time series, as a class, a label set, a per-pixel class or value, or object boxes and masks.
  > GEO-Bench-2 addresses this with a comprehensive framework spanning classification, segmentation, regression, object detection, and instance segmentation across 19 permissively-licensed datasets.
- `evaluation_method` = exact-match, classification-metric, domain-metric, statistical-fit, composite · [S4][geo-bench-s4]
  - why: GEO-Bench-2 fixes one metric per task type. Single-label accuracy is exact-match over a fixed label set; multi-label F1 is classification-metric; the Jaccard index (IoU) and mAP are domain-metric; RMSE on BioMassters' biomass maps is statistical-fit. Each capability score averages per-dataset scores normalised to \[0, 1\] across these methods, which is composite. GEO-Bench used accuracy and IoU and aggregated each task set the same way.
  > To report scores for a capability, we aggregate results across multiple datasets.
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model · [S1][geo-bench-s1]
  - why: Earth-observation foundation models and general vision backbones (ImageNet ConvNeXt, DINOv3) are each fine-tuned on the Earth-observation tasks, and that fine-tuning is the specialisation the benchmark tests; GEO-Bench-2 is the term's own example.
  > Since this is more representative of practical usage, we encourage users of the benchmark to report the results of fine-tuned models.

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S4][geo-bench-s4]
  - why: Splits are each dataset's own or spatially disjoint re-splits, not held out by sensor or region. GEO-Bench-2's appendix coarsens the test images' ground sample distance while training at the original one, a shifted condition, but as an ablation outside the scored protocol.
  > This ablation applies a 14x14 kernel filter to increase the Ground Sampling Distance (GSD) of validation and test images, while train images are kept at the original resolution.
- `capability` not `sample-efficiency` · [S1][geo-bench-s1]
  - why: GEO-Bench ships official training subsets from 1% to 100% and reports results by training size, but the headline protocol trains on the full split and GEO-Bench-2 drops the subsets.
  > As part of the benchmark, we also provide official subsets of the training sets with train ratios of (0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1)
- `evaluation_method` not `entrant-relative-ranking` · [S4][geo-bench-s4]
  - why: Scores are normalised against reference points computed once from the maintainers' fixed set of models, which every user reuses, so adding an entrant does not move the others' numbers.
  > These normalization factors, computed from our fixed set of models

Scores are normalised to \[0, 1\] against fixed reference points and aggregated by interquartile mean with a stratified bootstrap, per task set in GEO-Bench and per capability group in GEO-Bench-2.; tests_hidden_from_system false · [S1][geo-bench-s1]

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `versions`) The entry is GEO-Bench with GEO-Bench-2 as its second edition, as GEO-Bench's README calls it the successor and one ServiceNow researcher is the corresponding author of both. But the holder changed (ServiceNow to the AI Alliance), only three datasets carried over, and the stress corpus and taxonomy examples treat geo-bench-2 as its own id. It could instead be its own entry with lineage.supersedes. · [S8][geo-bench-s8]
   > GEO-Bench-2 is the successor to GEO-Bench, published by the AI Alliance
2. (field `comparability.material_extra`) Spatial resolution has no EvalConditions field, so it is recorded per task in subsets and reaches a claim only through subset\_used. Resizing, cropping or coarsening the images changes it and the score (GEO-Bench-2's GSD ablation; GEO-Bench's warning on crop-and-resize). A resolution field, or a ruling that subset\_used suffices, is needed; this task could not file a tag gap or write a conditions record. · [S4][geo-bench-s4]
   > Both figures highlight that increasing GSD tends to lower test metrics across all models.
3. (field `subsets`) Every per-task ground sample distance and sensor in subsets was read from the text layer of the two papers' tables, matched by row order to the name column. Check each against Table 1 (GEO-Bench) and Table 2 (GEO-Bench-2) in the PDFs. GEO-Bench gives the RGB bands' resolution only, and GEO-Bench-2 one value per dataset.
4. (field `data.dataset_licence`) Dataset licences are mixed and the sources disagree. Read in row order, GEO-Bench-2's Table 2 gives DynamicEarthNet CC-BY-4.0, PASTIS CC-BY-4.0, KuroSiwo MIT and SpaceNet2 CC-BY-SA-4.0, while the Hugging Face tags (API, 2026-10-14) give cc-by-sa-4.0, etalab-2.0, cc and cc-by-4.0. GEO-Bench's bundle is tagged cc-by-sa-4.0 as a whole against Table 1's per-task licences.
5. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type community-collective follows the stress corpus for the current edition; GEO-Bench was held by ServiceNow (industry-lab), and the AI Alliance's legal form was not looked up.
6. (field `activity`) accepting-submissions rests on the stated pull-request route, but the leaderboard's only result sets are the maintainers' own release runs, its repository was last pushed on 2026-01-19, and no outside submission was seen. · [S6][geo-bench-s6]
   > Create a pull request to main
7. (field `data.refresh`) GEO-Bench-2 is marked not frozen and refresh versioned-releases, but several of its Hugging Face datasets were modified in December 2025 and January 2026 (API lastModified), after the paper, with no version label stated for the change.
8. (field `governance.independence_flags`) The independence flag rests on IBM authors of TerraMind and Prithvi-EO-2.0 being GEO-Bench-2 authors (and, for GEO-Bench, ServiceNow's SeCo among the baselines); the rows are the paper's baselines, not models built for the board. · [S4][geo-bench-s4]
   > Some examples include TerraMind-V1-Large for its multi-spectral and Multi-Temporal capabilities
9. (field `capability`) sample-efficiency was rejected although GEO-Bench ships official training subsets (1% to 100%) and the paper reports results along them.

### 2.5 MapEval (mapeval)

`data/benchmarks/earth-climate/mapeval.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*Foundation models on 700 multiple-choice map questions, from Google Maps data given as text, API tools or snapshots.*

A benchmark of geo-spatial reasoning over map services: 700 multiple-choice questions about places in 180 cities and 54 countries, in three tasks. MapEval-Textual (300 questions) gives an LLM a long context fetched from Google Maps APIs (places, ratings, opening hours, distances, routes); MapEval-API asks the same 300 questions without the context, and a ReAct agent must query map tools served from a cached copy of the Google Maps responses (over 13,000 places); MapEval-Visual (400 questions) gives a VLM a Google Maps snapshot at zoom 8 to 21. Questions fall into Place Info, Nearby, Routing, Trip planning (text and API only), Counting (visual only) and Unanswerable, and each has 2 to 7 options (4.0 on average). Questions were written by the authors' team from the map data, with items most LLMs answered easily filtered out. Scoring is accuracy per task; no score spans the three tasks. Of 30 models the best is Claude-3.5-Sonnet on every task (66.33% textual, tied with Gemini-1.5-Pro; 64.00% API; 61.65% visual), against human scores of 86.67% (textual and API) and 82.23% (visual) from two team members' best attempts.

**Evidence** (48 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### mapeval · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][mapeval-s1]

  > Submitted on 31 Dec 2024 (v1), last revised 6 Jun 2025 (this version, v2)

#### mapeval · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary earth-climate/geospatial-reasoning; secondary multimodal/visual-qa, agents-tooluse/tool-api-calling · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: Every question asks about places and the spatial relations between them (direction, distance, proximity, routes, multi-stop trips), which is the leaf's definition, reasoning over geographic location and spatial relationships, and the benchmark's own claim is geo-spatial reasoning across its three tasks. The leaf has no examples or tests yet; no other family's example or exclusion names it. The reasoning-general family excludes reasoning applied to a field with its own family, and homographs.yaml puts geospatial spatial reasoning here rather than in reasoning-general. The task formats go to secondary - questions answered about a map image (visual-qa) and the agent's calls to map APIs (tool-api-calling).
  > no studies have rigorously tested the capabilities of foundation models in location or geo-spatial reasoning
- `capability` = spatial-reasoning · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: Answers turn on directions, straight-line distances, nearest places and route choices that must be worked out from coordinates, distances or the map, not read off; the paper's error analysis names distances and cardinal directions as the main failures.
  > In spatial reasoning, they often fail with straight-line distances (Listing 1), cardinal directions
- `capability` = tool-use · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: In MapEval-API the agent must choose among map tools (place search, place details, nearby search, directions, travel time), fill their parameters and use what they return; wrong parameters and request loops are the reported failure modes, so the score depends on the calls.
  > Incorrect parameter usage results in failures, such as missing key parameters, using incompatible values, or entering infinite request loops when no valid results are found.
- `capability` = context-integration · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: MapEval-Textual supplies the map data the answer depends on, and the answer key was built from that same context; Unanswerable items score recognising that the supplied context does not settle the question.
  > The ground truth answers were derived from the same context.
- `capability` = temporal-reasoning · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: Trip and Place Info questions depend on opening hours, visit durations and travel times, such as fitting a three-hour museum visit, a coffee break and a park visit into an afternoon.
  > Temporal reasoning challenges include inefficient trip planning and errors in travel times or visit durations
- `capability` = perception · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: MapEval-Visual's 400 questions give a map snapshot and score what is recovered from it - labelled places, ratings shown on the map, symbols, routes and counts of marked places.
  > MapEval-Visual task requires the model to interpret and analyze map snapshots, specifically digital map views from services like Google Maps.
- `evaluation_method` = multiple-choice · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: Every item is scored by whether the chosen option is the key, and each task's score is accuracy over its items. Options per item run from 2 (yes/no) to 7, 4.004 on average, so the chance rate varies by item and is about 25% on average; the paper does not state a chance baseline.
  > We evaluate all tasks using the accuracy metric, defined as the percentage of correct choices selected by the model.
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model, model-in-benchmark-harness · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: MapEval-Textual and MapEval-Visual prompt each LLM or VLM directly with the context or image, the question and the options (instruction-tuned-model). MapEval-API runs every LLM inside the same zero-shot ReAct agent with the benchmark's tools and prompts, so only the model varies (model-in-benchmark-harness).
  > We assess LLMs for MapEval-Textual, VLMs for MapEval-Visual, and ReACT agents

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `earth-climate/remote-sensing` · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: The images are rendered digital map views with labels, routes and icons, not satellite or airborne imagery, and the paper sets its visual task apart from remote sensing.
  > this approach differs significantly from the task of reasoning over interactive digital map views
- `domain` not `reasoning-general/planning` · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: Trip questions ask for a multi-stop schedule, but they are 67 of the 300 text questions and are answered by picking an option; plan construction is not the benchmark's subject.
  > MapEval-Textual and MapEval-API exclusively feature Trip questions, which involve planning multi-stop journeys across various POIs.
- `capability` not `honesty` · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: Unanswerable questions (20 per task) reward recognising insufficient information, but that is one option among the others, scored as accuracy like any other, not truthfulness scored separately from correctness (see review\_checks).
  > MapEval includes questions where context is insufficient to provide an answer
- `capability` not `knowledge-recall` · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: Some questions need general knowledge (52 commonsense items in MapEval-Visual), but the answers come from the supplied map data, which is context-integration.
  > there are 52 commonsense QAs in MapEval-Visual
- `evaluation_method` not `model-graded-judge` · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: An appendix experiment removes the options and grades Claude-3.5-Sonnet's free answers with o3-mini; it is a robustness check, not the benchmark's protocol, and the paper keeps the multiple-choice format.
  > The outputs were automatically graded using the o3-mini model.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `agent-scaffold` · [S1][mapeval-s1]
  - why: Later papers bring their own agents to MapEval-API (Spatial-Agent, MapAgent), and the paper itself tries Chameleon on GPT-3.5-Turbo, but the designed protocol is the benchmark's own ReAct loop; entrant scaffolds are recorded under as\_used.
  > Chameleon 54.69 54.21 51.51 43.28 25.00 49.33

(field `domain.primary`) Primary domain: geospatial-reasoning follows the leaf's definition and the benchmark's claim, but the earth-climate family's inclusion test asks for an Earth-system quantity (weather, climate, land surface, hazard, ecology, energy), and MapEval's subject is human geography on a commercial map service - places, ratings, opening hours and routes. Either the family's test should admit geospatial reasoning over the built environment or the leaf belongs in another family; no other family names such a benchmark. · [S1][mapeval-s1]

(field `data.data_provenance`) data\_provenance expert-authored rests on the paper calling its annotator an expert; the annotators are the authors' team, and if they count as non-specialists answering everyday map questions, crowd-authored applies. 6. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark rests on MapAgent, a later paper by four of the eight authors that reports gains on MapEval; the release paper evaluates none of the authors' own models. · [S4][mapeval-s4]

### 2.6 WildfireSpreadTS (wildfirespreadts)

`data/benchmarks/earth-climate/wildfirespreadts.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*Next-day active fire maps for 607 US wildfires from daily 23-channel time series, scored by AP over held-out years.*

A dataset and benchmark for predicting how an active wildfire will spread over the next 24 hours, released by KTH Royal Institute of Technology with a NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks paper. It holds 607 fire events in the western contiguous United States from 2018 to 2021, chosen from the GlobFire burned-area database (fires over 1,000 hectares with VIIRS detections), as 13,607 daily images of 23 channels resampled to 375 m: the VIIRS active fire map, VIIRS reflectance bands, NDVI and EVI2, GRIDMET weather, drought and fire-danger variables, GFS weather forecasts, land cover, and elevation, slope and aspect. Each event is a time series with four buffer days before and after the GlobFire dates. The task is to predict the next day's binarised VIIRS active fire map, a proxy for the true fire spread, from one day or five days of observations. Models are scored by test-set average precision of the fire class over all test pixels, as the mean and standard deviation of a 12-fold cross-validation over every assignment of the four years to training (two years), validation and test, with every test series starting at its sixth day. The paper's baselines are fire persistence, logistic regression, a ResNet-18 U-Net, a ConvLSTM and UTAE; UTAE with five days of vegetation features scores best (AP 0.372), and persistence scores 0.193. Fire pixels are about 0.1% of the total, and the labels carry noise from smoke, clouds and detection errors. Later papers report on the same protocol; WSTS+ (2025) raised the best AP to about 0.48 and extended the data to 2016-2023.

#### wildfirespreadts · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary earth-climate/hazard-prediction; secondary earth-climate/remote-sensing · [S1][wildfirespreadts-s1]
  - why: The scored quantity is where an active wildfire will be burning the next day, predicted before it is observed; hazard-prediction's definition names wildfires, and remote-sensing's exclusion test sends a task that forecasts an event before it happens to hazard-prediction. The inputs and the labels are satellite and gridded Earth-observation products and the paper presents the dataset as remote sensing, so remote-sensing is secondary.
  > We present a multi-temporal, multi-modal remote-sensing dataset for predicting how active wildfires will spread at a resolution of 24 hours.
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S3][wildfirespreadts-s3]
  - why: Models predict the future state of an Earth-system process, the next day's active fire extent, from measurements of the fire, fuel, weather and topography, and the score compares the prediction with the satellite detections of that day.
  > predict the output of the VIIRS active fire product, as a proxy for predicting the actual ground truth fire spread
- `evaluation_method` = classification-metric · [S3][wildfirespreadts-s3]
  - why: Average precision, the area under the precision-recall curve of per-pixel fire scores against the binarised next-day map, is a general statistic of a score ranking; the F1 score reported for the persistence baseline is one too. The inclusion test names AUPRC and F1.
  > To evaluate models, we use the test set average precision (AP).
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model, classical-algorithm · [S3][wildfirespreadts-s3]
  - why: The benchmark is built for deep networks trained from scratch on its data for wildfire spread prediction, a task fire and Earth science define (the paper's U-Net, ConvLSTM and UTAE, and later papers' U-Nets, SegFormer and SwinUnet). Fire persistence, which predicts that today's fire map holds tomorrow, has no learned component and is scored as a baseline in the same tables.
  > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `physics/simulation-surrogates` · [S3][wildfirespreadts-s3]
  - why: The paper sets its task apart from networks trained to approximate fire simulators such as FARSITE; models learn from satellite observations and are scored against observed detections, not against a simulator.
  > Such simulators have been used to generate training data, and train neural networks to approximate the spread predictions made by the simulators
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S3][wildfirespreadts-s3]
  - why: Each test fold is a held-out year, and the paper chose cross-validation over years because yearly distributions differ, but the 12 folds are pooled into one mean and no shifted condition is scored on its own, as for cy-bench's leave-one-year-out. WSTS+ later measured the cross-year shift (see review\_checks).
  > This is necessary, because of the large differences between the yearly data distributions

(field `domain`) hazard-prediction has no inclusion test or examples yet; this entry is its first primary use, on the definition (which names wildfires) and remote-sensing's exclusion test for forecasting an event. remote-sensing is secondary because the dataset presents itself as remote sensing; vision/segmentation was rejected though the models are segmentation networks.
2. (field `capability`, needs a specialist) distribution-shift-generalization was rejected because the 12 year-folds are pooled into one mean, as for cy-bench. The paper chose year folds for their differing distributions, and WSTS+ reports significant cross-year shift and per-year scores; a specialist may read the held-out year as a deliberate shift. · [S4][wildfirespreadts-s4]
   > We discover and analyze significant cross-year domain shift, a critical challenge for the field.
3. (field `as_used`) The sources disagree on how the paper's models were selected. The paper says it kept the model with the highest validation loss (probably meaning the best), WSTS+ says the original U-Net was selected on validation F1; selection on validation AP is one of WSTS+'s gains. · [S3][wildfirespreadts-s3]
   > We keep the model with the highest validation loss, evaluated after each training epoch
4. (field `comparability`) A data-loader bug was fixed after the paper (commit ab3c8f3), and the README says scores rise slightly; whether WSTS+ ran the corrected loader, and so whether its numbers sit beside the paper's on equal terms, was not checked. harness is named material for this reason. · S6
   > the corrected dataset class leads to slightly higher performance, but the trends in the results are basically the same as those reported in the paper
5. (field `comparability`) The number of input days and the feature set change every score and have no EvalConditions field, so claims that differ on them can share a comparability key. No EvalConditions record was written (this task may not write data/conditions/); the proposed reference is lead\_time one day, all 12 folds, five input days and the vegetation features. · [S3][wildfirespreadts-s3]
   > Multi includes vegetation, land cover, topography and weather features.
6. (field `designed_for_subjects`) classical-algorithm rests on fire persistence, the only non-learned row in the tables (logistic regression is learned). Drop it if a baseline that simple should not count as a designed-for entrant.
7. (field `paper`) The paper's DOI (10.52202/075280-3258, Curran's proceedings) was taken from the abstract page and not resolved. The PDF Source carries no DOI and is withheld from archiving for the authors' e-mail addresses, and the abstract page is pending; whether the PDF Source should carry the DOI instead, which would make it citable without a capture.
8. (field `data.data_provenance`) data\_provenance tags GRIDMET and the GFS forecasts as simulation-generated beside real-world-instrument, and GlobFire as curated-public-database because the events were selected from it; whether the predictors' provenance belongs in the field is a judgement, as for cy-bench.
9. (field `data.refresh`) refresh static rests on one Zenodo version and the datasheet's plan of no regular updates; the record was modified on 2024-07-11 without a new version, and what changed was not checked. · [S2][wildfirespreadts-s2]
   > Modified July 11, 2024
10. (field `ground_truth_source`) The ground truth is the VIIRS active fire product, which the paper names a proxy for the real spread; the abstract lists smoke, clouds and detection errors as label noise, and the datasheet warns against using the data as ground truth for statistics of fire spread. · [S1][wildfirespreadts-s1]
   > d) noisy labels, due to smoke, clouds, and inaccuracies in the active fire detection

### 2.7 LifeCLEF (lifeclef)

`data/benchmarks/earth-climate/lifeclef.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*CLEF's yearly biodiversity AI lab, species identification in images, sound and text in Kaggle-hosted tasks.*

A lab of CLEF, the Conference and Labs of the Evaluation Forum, that runs machine-learning challenges on biodiversity every year, since 2014 by its own overview page and since 2011 by its 2025 overview. Each edition is a set of independent tasks, each with its own data, metric and ranking, and the line-up changes from year to year. The 2026 edition had five: AnimalCLEF (clustering photographs of loggerhead sea turtles and Texas horned lizards into individual animals, scored by the adjusted Rand index), BirdCLEF+ (identifying 234 bird, amphibian, insect, mammal and reptile taxa in 5-second windows of Pantanal soundscapes, scored by macro-averaged ROC-AUC), FathomNetCLEF (object detection in underwater images trained on incompletely labelled data, scored by mAP), PestCLEF (document-level relation extraction on plant pests from web documents, scored by F-score) and PlantCLEF (identifying every plant species in high-resolution vegetation-plot images, scored by F1 averaged per transect). The 2024 and 2025 editions also ran GeoLifeCLEF (species presence prediction from occurrence and remote-sensing data) and FungiCLEF, and 2024 SnakeCLEF. Every 2026 task ran as a Kaggle competition ranked on a private leaderboard against labels the organisers withheld; BirdCLEF+ was a code competition whose notebooks ran on hidden test audio, CPU-only and within 90 minutes. Results appear in the CLEF Working Notes (CEUR-WS) and a lab overview in Springer's LNCS. The lab makes a working note describing each run mandatory, and four of the 2026 task pages rank officially only teams that submitted one. A weakness the sources name: BirdCLEF+ 2026's top 20 teams fell within about 0.010 ROC-AUC, which its organisers say may not separate them beyond the error of the evaluation split.

#### lifeclef · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][lifeclef-s1]

#### lifeclef · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary earth-climate/ecology-biodiversity; secondary audio-speech/bioacoustics, vision/classification, vision/detection, language/information-extraction; per_edition true · [S1][lifeclef-s1]
  - why: The lab's own claim is biodiversity across modalities (photographs, soundscapes, underwater images, web text), which is the primary's inclusion test and its own lifeclef-2026 example; every task scores identifying or understanding species.
  > The 2026 edition of LifeCLEF proposes five data-oriented challenges related to the identification and understanding of biodiversity
- `capability` = perception · [S4][lifeclef-s4]
  - why: Four of the five 2026 tasks score what was recovered from a raw signal, photographs, soundscape audio or underwater images (the subsets carry the per-task split).
  > identifying both the presence and location of marine organisms across diverse habitats
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S5][lifeclef-s5]
  - why: PlantCLEF trains on close-ups of single plants and scores vegetation-plot images with the same species label set, and BirdCLEF+ trains mainly on focal recordings and scores field soundscapes; the label set stays and only the inputs move, the term's tie-break against transfer-learning.
  > The main difficulty of the task lies in the shift between the test data (high-resolution multi-label images of vegetation plots) and the training data (single-label images of individual plants).
- `capability` = context-integration · [S6][lifeclef-s6]
  - why: PestCLEF supplies the web documents and scores the relations extracted from them, so the supplied text determines the answer.
  > The task is a knowledge graph extraction task and is framed as a document-level relation extraction problem.
- `evaluation_method` = classification-metric, domain-metric · [S7][lifeclef-s7]
  - why: Four 2026 tasks are scored by general-purpose statistics of predicted labels, scores or clusters, AnimalCLEF by the adjusted Rand index, BirdCLEF+ by macro-averaged ROC-AUC, PestCLEF by F-score and PlantCLEF by sample F1 averaged per transect (classification-metric); FathomNetCLEF by detection mAP (domain-metric). Each subset carries its own metric's quote.
  > The evaluation metric was a variant of macro-averaged ROC-AUC computed on 5-second soundscape clips, excluding classes with no true positive labels in the private test set.
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model · [S8][lifeclef-s8]
  - why: Entrants are models built or fine-tuned for species identification and biodiversity monitoring, tasks the ecology discipline defines; AnimalCLEF and PlantCLEF supply pretrained domain models, and the leading BirdCLEF+ entries distil Perch 2.0, a bioacoustic foundation model.
  > This competition focuses on the development of machine learning models that identify wildlife species from passive acoustic monitoring (PAM).

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `earth-climate/remote-sensing` · [S3][lifeclef-s3]
  - why: GeoLifeCLEF (2024, 2025) used high-resolution remote sensing, but as predictors of species presence, which the term's exclusion sends to the target's own leaf; no 2026 task uses overhead imagery.
  > (iii) GeoLifeCLEF 2025: species presence prediction based on species occurrences and high-resolution remote sensing data
- `capability` not `calibration-uncertainty` · [S7][lifeclef-s7]
  - why: BirdCLEF+ and FathomNetCLEF consume per-class scores, but through rank-based ROC-AUC and mAP, chosen so that no threshold or calibration is assessed.
  > using rank-based metrics like ROC-AUC helps standardize performance assessments without requiring species-specific threshold calibration
- `designed_for_subjects` not `agent-scaffold` · [S7][lifeclef-s7]
  - why: Some 2026 BirdCLEF+ entries were built with AI coding agents, one by an autonomous agent loop, but what is submitted and scored is the trained model in a notebook, not the agent.
  > A notable development in this edition of the challenge was the adoption of AI coding agents

(field `governance.submission_process`) BirdCLEF+'s Kaggle notebooks are tagged containerized-algorithm-submission, as arc-agi-3's entry reads Kaggle notebooks; by the sandboxed-rerun examples (a plugin is not a container image) they could be sandboxed-rerun. publication-gated rests on the lab's mandatory working notes and four task pages, while the BirdCLEF+ page only encourages a working note. · [S8][lifeclef-s8]

8. (field `data.access`) data.access is train-open-test-held-out for the family, but BirdCLEF+'s test audio never leaves Kaggle, which alone is private-test-server. · [S7][lifeclef-s7]
   > The challenge was hosted on Kaggle in a code competition format with hidden test data.
9. The three CEUR-WS papers are withheld from archiving for their authors' e-mail contact lines, as the curation rule for personal data asks, although CEUR-WS already publishes them permanently under a URN; a reviewer may prefer to archive them.
10. (field `execution.compute_tier`) compute\_tier is null because the tasks differ; BirdCLEF+ alone would be provided-allocation (Kaggle's CPU-only notebooks), and no source states what the other tasks cost an entrant.

### 2.8 CY-Bench (cy-bench)

`data/benchmarks/earth-climate/cy-bench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Pre-harvest maize and wheat yield forecasts for subnational regions of over 25 countries, scored leave-one-year-out.*

A dataset and benchmark for forecasting end-of-season maize and wheat yields per subnational region before harvest, built by AgML, the machine-learning team of AgMIP, and held by Wageningen University & Research. The targets are official yield statistics at the finest administrative level each country publishes, from US counties and Brazilian municipalities to provinces: 38 countries for maize and 29 for wheat in the 2026 paper. Each kind of predictor comes from one global source, harmonised and aggregated over each region's cropland: AgERA5 weather, GLDAS soil moisture, JRC fPAR, MODIS NDVI and WISE soil properties, with ESA WorldCereal crop masks and crop calendars. A forecast is made at a lead time before harvest, the middle of the season by default, with every time series cut there. Models are trained and scored per crop and country by leave-one-year-out cross-validation, with NRMSE, MAPE and R2 computed by the cybench Python library. The maintainers' baseline tables (data v1.8, March 2025) list an average-yield model and a linear trend beside random-forest and ridge regressions; for maize the average-yield model has the lowest NRMSE over all countries. Results by others appear in their own papers.

- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S1][cy-bench-s1]
  - why: Models predict a property of an agricultural system, a region's end-of-season yield, from measurements of its weather, soil moisture, vegetation and soil, and the score compares the prediction with the yield the statistics office reported.
  > forecasting refers to the production of end-of-season yield estimates with a certain lead time before harvest (e.g., mid-season or 30 d before harvest)
- `evaluation_method` = statistical-fit · [S1][cy-bench-s1]
  - why: NRMSE (the RMSE divided by the test set's mean yield), MAPE and R2 are general goodness-of-fit statistics on continuous yields.

- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model, classical-algorithm · [S4][cy-bench-s4]
  - why: The benchmark compares data-driven yield models trained from scratch on its own per-country data, for a task agronomy defines. The maintainers' tables rank random-forest and ridge models beside two non-learned baselines, an average-yield model and a linear trend, scored the same way.
  > AverageYieldModel \| LinearTrend \| RFRes \| RidgeRes \| SklearnRF \| SklearnRidge

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `earth-climate/weather-forecasting` · [S1][cy-bench-s1]
  - why: Weather enters as observed predictors cut at the forecast date; no atmospheric state is forecast, and weather forecasts are left out of the inputs.
  > We did not include weather forecasts in CY-Bench because the evidence supporting their usefulness is variable
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S1][cy-bench-s1]
  - why: Leave-one-year-out holds out each year in turn and pools every fold into one score, to stop correlated yields of the same year leaking into training. No input is drawn deliberately from a shifted distribution and scored as a condition of its own.
  > LOYO avoids this by holding out an entire year, ensuring that correlations within that year are only encountered during evaluation.
- `capability` not `transfer-learning` · [S1][cy-bench-s1]
  - why: The paper names transfer learning and domain adaptation as research the dataset enables, not as part of its protocol, which trains and tests within one crop and country.
  > CY-Bench enables explorations in transfer learning, domain adaptation, and representation learning
- `capability` not `probabilistic-forecasting` · [S3][cy-bench-s3]
  - why: The yields of every evaluated year already exist and are in the dataset; the forecasts are point estimates of past seasons, and no probability is scored.
  > we evaluate models using predictors and yield statistics for all available years
- `designed_for_subjects` not `scientific-surrogate-model` · [S1][cy-bench-s1]
  - why: The models do not stand in for a crop simulation or a solver. They are scored against reported yields, and the paper sets them apart from process-based crop models.
  > Traditionally, crop yield prediction has been based on biophysical process based crop models

### 2.9 Learning to Run a Power Network (L2RPN) (l2rpn)

`data/benchmarks/earth-climate/l2rpn.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*RTE's competition series since 2019 in which agents operate a simulated power grid through weekly Grid2Op scenarios.*

A series of competitions run since 2019 by RTE, the French transmission system operator, with ChaLearn and partners, in which an agent operates a simulated power transmission grid in real time. Each scenario plays production, consumption and maintenance time series ("chronics") at five-minute steps; the agent observes the full grid state at every step and may change the grid's topology (bus splitting at substations, line switching), redispatch generators and, from 2022, curtail renewables and use batteries, under operational rules such as cooldowns and limits on simultaneous actions. Overloaded lines trip, which can cascade, and the episode ends in a game over when demand is no longer met. Agents are submitted as code to CodaLab and run on scenarios the participants never see. The score per scenario comes from the episode's operational cost, normalised so that -100 is an immediate blackout, 0 the do-nothing agent, 80 a completed scenario and 100 a further 20% cost saving; the leaderboard averages it over the test scenarios. The first edition (IJCNN 2019) used the IEEE 14-bus grid on the pypownet platform. From WCCI 2020 the series runs on Grid2Op, RTE's open-source simulator, on parts of the IEEE 118-bus grid: NeurIPS 2020 had a robustness track against an adversarial opponent that disconnects loaded lines and an adaptability track over unseen energy mixes; ICAPS 2021 added alarms for a human operator; WCCI 2022 moved to a near carbon-free 2050 energy mix with batteries; and a 2023 edition funded by the Ile-de-France region used a 2035 mix with a three-area opponent. TU Delft ran the 2022 environment again in 2023. Winning entries have mixed reinforcement learning, imitation, search and expert rules.

**Evidence** (50 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### l2rpn · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
  > challenge is a series of competitions that model the sequential decision-making environments of real-time power network operations
- `release_venue` = IJCNN 2019 · [S2][l2rpn-s2]
  > After a successful first competition at IJCNN 2019 on a reduced version of our proposed challenge, two new competitions will run this year 2020 at WCCI and NeurIPS.

#### l2rpn · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary earth-climate/energy-systems · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
  - why: The scored act is operating a power transmission grid, which the subdomain's definition names ("optimising energy generation, demand or grid operation"), and the family admits an energy control task as its own example (smart-buildings-challenge). games-planning was weighed, since scores come from episodes against an environment that responds, but none of its leaves fits a grid simulator and the taxonomy places operated energy systems here.
  > The goal of this competition was to control a power network to maintain a supply of electricity to consumers on the network over a given time horizon by avoiding a blackout.
- `capability` = optimization · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
  - why: The ranked quantity is the scenario's operational cost (energy losses, redispatching and the cost of a blackout), normalised per scenario, and 20 of the 100 points reward lowering it beyond merely surviving. The 2022 score keeps the same three costs.
  > The score per scenario was based on the cumulative network operational cost
- `capability` = long-horizon-execution · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
  - why: One scored episode is a week of 2,016 five-minute steps (2019's were one to three days), the agent acts on state its own earlier actions produced (topology, cooldowns), and a game over ends the scenario with the blackout's cost, so full success is out of reach after it.
  > Environments are episodic, running at 5-minute resolution over a week (2016 timesteps).
- `capability` = adversarial-robustness · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
  - why: In the NeurIPS 2020 robustness track an automated opponent picks lines to disconnect among the most loaded, and the score is how well the agent keeps the grid running through the attacks; the ICAPS 2021, WCCI 2022 and 2023 environments keep an opponent, which in 2023 attacks three areas at once.
  > The opponent was heuristically designed, disconnecting one of the most loaded lines at random times
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
  - why: The NeurIPS 2020 adaptability track trained on five known energy-mix distributions (10% to 30% renewables) and tested on unknown ones, one slightly outside the training range, with the task and score unchanged; only the inputs move.
  > At test time however, the agents had to respond to unknown energy mix distributions within the 1x-3x range.
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
  - why: Each episode runs in the grid simulator and is scored on a bounded scale against fixed anchors, the do-nothing agent at 0 and a completed scenario at 80, with -100 for an immediate blackout and a time cap that scores -100 beyond it; the leaderboard averages the scenarios.
  > \[-100,0,80,100\] = \[initial blackout, do-nothing agent score, scenario completed, additional 20%operational cost optimization\]
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy, classical-algorithm · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
  - why: The series was built to bring reinforcement learning to grid operation, and most winners are RL agents, but expert systems and optimisation agents enter on the same score and place high (the second of the 2020 adaptability track, and the second and third of 2022 per the survey, used no learning).
  > This sets bounds on the added value of Machine Learning on those problems.
- `secondary_axes` = latency · [S9][l2rpn-s9]
  - why: The 2019 leaderboard reported each agent's computation time beside its score, and every edition read caps run time, so slow search-based agents trade score against time.
  > 1a Final leaderboard of the L2RPN competition with cumulated scores and computation time

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `calibration-uncertainty` · [S3][l2rpn-s3]
  - why: The ICAPS 2021 edition scored alarms raised before a failure, a confidence signal, but only in that edition; the series' score does not consume a stated probability.
  > the agent can raise an alarm when the assistance of an operator is needed due to a risk of failure
- `designed_for_subjects` not `multi-agent-system` · [S4][l2rpn-s4]
  - why: Artelys's 2023 entry combined specialised agents, but the environment is single-agent and each team submits one controller.
  > Our solution is based on a multi-agent cooperation framework where specialised agents based on different technologies (Reinforcement Learning, Optimisation and Expert System)

#### l2rpn · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system Baidu's RL agent (team RL\_agent), PARL policy trained by evolutionary black-box optimisation over a reduced action set · [S1][l2rpn-s1]

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system SoftGNN90% N-1 (graph-based soft-label imitation learning) · [S5][l2rpn-s5]
  > achieved the highest overall performance with a mean L2RPN score of 44.43
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = false · [S8][l2rpn-s8]
  - why: Each edition's official scores came from hidden test scenarios run by the organisers on CodaLab, now phased out. The simulator and training environments are open, and the 2022 test environment is now used by others, so a third party can rerun the 2022 protocol but not the other editions' rankings.
  > RL agents capable of controlling the power network will be blind tested on the platform with new scenarios not known to the participants.
- `task.item_definition` = One scenario, a week of five-minute steps (2,016) from 2020 on, played until it ends or a game over. · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
  > The Game Over condition is triggered if total demand is not met anymore, that is if some consumption is lost at a substation.
- `task` = exists true; input at every five-minute step, the complete observed state of the grid -- flows and usage of each line, production and consumption at each node, topology, line disconnection and maintenance durations -- and a simulate() call to test an action on the current state; output One action per step, possibly none -- topology changes (bus splitting, line switching) and generator redispatching, and from 2022 renewable curtailment and storage -- within the rules on how often and how much may change at once.; scoring Per scenario, the episode's operational cost normalised to \[-100, 100\] (-100 immediate blackout, 0 the do-nothing agent, 80 a completed scenario, 100 a further 20% saving); the leaderboard averages the hidden test scenarios (24 weekly scenarios per NeurIPS 2020 track) under a run-time cap (20 minutes in 2019, 30 in 2020). The 2019 edition scored line margins instead.; tests_hidden_from_system true; item_definition One scenario, a week of five-minute steps (2,016) from 2020 on, played until it ends or a game over. · [S1][l2rpn-s1]

- `execution.compute_tier` = simulator-required · [S12][l2rpn-s12]
  - why: Scoring an agent means playing its episodes through the grid simulator, whatever the agent.

- `execution.harness` = Grid2Op (its environments per edition, the Runner, and the L2RPN baselines), with each edition's starting kit on CodaLab · [S12][l2rpn-s12]
  > how to use the \`Runner\` class to assess how well an agent is performing rapidly
- `execution.submission_channel` · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
  > The competition eventually ran smoothly on Codalab competition platform
- `aggregation_policy` = official-aggregate · [S1][l2rpn-s1]
